newsitem.title: USA: U.S. plans to seek delay of next loan to Croatia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. plans to seek delay of next loan to Croatia.

text.p: The United States plans to seek postponement of a $30 million World Bank loan to Croatia because Zagreb has not followed through on Dayton peace accord commitments, a U.S. official said on Monday.
"Our current view is that this loan should not be allowed to go forward," the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Reuters.

The position was disclosed after several influential Democratic and Republican senators wrote Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to express "deep disappointment" over a U.S. decision to back a $13 million World Bank loan to Croatia on June 10 and to urge opposition to the $30 million loan.

"We believe the arrest and transfer to The Hague of indicted war criminals needs to be treated as a more urgent priority," the senators said in a letter dated June 19. "The U.S. should oppose and work against such assistance to Croatia until it apprehends and transfers indicted war criminals who are in territory within its control," they said.

Democrats signing the letter were Patrick Leahy of Vermont, Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey, Dianne Feinstein of California and Barbara Mikulski of Maryland. Republicans were Richard Lugar of Indiana and Alfonse D'Amato of New York.

The United States has been reviewing international financial assistance to Croatia more rigorously since Albright announced last month that Washington was serious about conditioning aid on compliance with the 1995 Dayton peace accords that ended the Bosnia war and on other demands.

Despite its much-publicised threats, the United States decided this month to support a $13 million loan to Croatia from the International Finance Corporation, the private sector arm of the World Bank. Officials said the decision had been taken because of actions by Croatian President Franjo Tudjman that met demands made by Albright.

These included a decision to open a long-closed bridge at Brcko between Croatia and Bosnia, a new burst of support for a strengthened Croat-Moslem federation in Bosnia and orders for the arrest of several people suspected of brutalizing Serbs who tried to return to their prewar homes in Croatia.

But the U.S. official said on Monday Washington would seek to hold up the $30 million loan this month because Tudjman "has not followed through on some of his commitments, including not taking the necessary steps on war criminals."

Individuals wanted for war crimes are "coming in and out of Croatia and in and out of Croatian-controlled territory in Bosnia," he said. He described the U.S. approach as carefully calibrated to show the Croatians that they can expect positive reinforcement from the international community when they meet their commitments and negative consequences when they renege.

"We intend to send concrete signals on a weekly and monthly basis," the official said. "Right now, in our view, they need to receive a signal that they haven't continued the path toward progress," he added.

Croatia extradited its first war crimes suspect to the international war crimes tribunal in The Hague in April, days after the West tightened its pressure. Since then, "there has not been real movement (on war crimes) by Croatia," the U.S. official said. But he stressed that aid decisions would not be based on only one issue.
